## TL;DR

Review round 1 exposed two remaining defects. A cleanup signal that failed with EPERM was swallowed, but the liveness poll continued to report the group as alive and could wait forever. Fatal marker writing also used a hardcoded `.repoos` directory while boot recovery used the configured cache directory. The cleanup now stops promptly when the group is gone or cannot be signalled, the crash marker path is shared by writer and reader, and regressions cover signal EPERM, probe EPERM, and an injected `unhandledRejection` event.

## Work and rationale

The first implementation correctly contained an EPERM from `process.kill`, but review demonstrated that containing the exception was not enough. `processGroupAlive` intentionally treated EPERM as proof that a process group existed. That is useful for some existence checks, but it is unsafe as the termination loop condition: a caller without permission cannot make progress and cannot confirm teardown. I changed that probe to return false on EPERM and made `terminateProcessGroupAndWait` stop as soon as its signal call returns ESRCH or EPERM. Other failures continue to reject so genuine unexpected errors remain visible.

The new process-group regression cases cover both locations where EPERM can occur. A denied SIGTERM signal resolves immediately without entering the polling loop. A successful SIGTERM followed by a denied liveness probe also resolves immediately. Both cases check diagnostic output with the target group leader PID. The earlier integration boundary around the process-level rejection handler now has a test that actually emits `unhandledRejection` with an injected EPERM error and asserts that `process.exit` is not called.

For the crash marker, the handler and startup had independently constructed their paths. The handler assumed `.repoos`; startup used `config.cacheDir`. I introduced one path helper and used it for both sides, then added a test with a non-default cache directory. This makes the next-boot attention notice available when a repository customizes its cache location.

The incident documentation now includes the review-discovered poll hang alongside the original crash cause. The engineer report draft records the decisions and test outcomes for RepoOS to bind to the checked tree.

## Approaches tried

I reproduced the reviewer’s narrow scenario with mocked `process.kill` calls instead of waiting for a real foreign process group. This made the loop behavior deterministic and directly checked both the initial signal and later liveness-probe failure. I used an injected process event to test the registered handler’s behavior instead of testing only the error classifier. I centralized marker path construction rather than adjusting only one of the two call sites.

## Challenges and blockers

The original incident log was not present in the worktree, so the specific production caller could not be confirmed from the stack trace. The failure mode was independently reproduced at the shared process-group cleanup helper used by validation, handoff, close-out and check execution. RepoOS remote validation did not complete its incremental upload, so the requested scoped check completed its changed-path test run locally. The scoped suite passed all 283 files (4,697 tests passed, 9 skipped), including the added process-group, unhandled-rejection, attention notice, and close-out cleanup regressions. The UI smoke and rendered-contrast checks passed. The check finished with all selected steps green, including format, lint, build, safety scans and task-asset validation. An earlier check attempt had infrastructure and timing failures; the final check on the corrected tree passed.

## Key learnings

A failed signal and a liveness probe that returns EPERM must agree on the cleanup policy. Treating one as recoverable while the other insists the target is alive creates an infinite wait. Tests for process-level resilience should exercise the actual event handler path, not only its classifier. Durable restart evidence also needs one canonical path derived from configuration so the writer and next boot cannot silently diverge.
